Sugar, Slaves, and the Atlantic World

The Triangle Trade and the Middle Passage

Mini-lesson · Mr. Magister

Following the Triangle

1Europe: ships loaded with goods
2Africa: goods traded for captives
3The Americas: captives sold
4Home: sugar and tobacco sold
Today's Focus

How did the Atlantic slave trade work, who took part in it, and how did a small group of people turn the world against it?

Last lesson ended with planters who needed workers and were willing to buy them. Today you will follow the trade that supplied them: how it worked, who took part, what the voyage was like, and how a small group of people finally turned the world against it.

Objectives
  1. Explain how the Atlantic slave trade worked and what role African states and European merchants played in it.
  2. Describe the Middle Passage and the conditions enslaved people faced.
  3. Trace the movement that ended the slave trade in the British Empire.
Quick Check-in

The planters needed workers who would not run out. Before you read: what do you think made the Atlantic slave trade so large?

    The Triangle Trade and the Middle Passage

    Part 1

    A New Scale

    Chapter 1A New Scale
    Chapter 1

    A New Scale

    Slavery was not new. It existed in ancient Greece and Rome, across Africa, and throughout the Mediterranean and the Islamic world. What the sugar colonies created was different in scale and in kind. In the Atlantic system, slavery was passed down from mother to child and tied to African ancestry. It was backed by law, and it was organized to produce goods for a market. Millions of people were bought to work on plantations, usually for life.

    The Atlantic trade grew out of older ones. Portuguese ships began bringing captives from the West African coast to Portugal in the 1440s, and a chronicler wrote an eyewitness account of one of the first large sales, held in the town of Lagos in 1444. The colonies then turned a practice into a rule of law. A Virginia law of 1662 declared that a child born to an enslaved mother was also enslaved, whoever the father was. Under that rule, a person could be born into bondage and could not leave it by any act of his or her own.

    Part 2

    Africa and the First Ships

    Chapter 2Africa and the First Ships
    Chapter 2

    Africa and the First Ships

    The Portuguese began buying captives on the West African coast in the 1440s, and in 1482 they built a fort at Elmina, in what is now Ghana, to protect the trade. Africans were not passive in what followed. Powerful states such as Asante and Dahomey sold captives to European ships, often prisoners from their own wars. The Europeans mostly stayed near the coast, partly because tropical diseases killed them and partly because African rulers did not allow them inland. Merchants paid in cloth, iron, guns, and shells. The guns made the wars that produced more captives.

    Dealings on the coast were bargaining sessions between traders who knew what they wanted. African merchants and rulers set the terms, and they often refused goods they did not like. Europeans brought cotton cloth from India, iron bars, brass goods, guns, and cowrie shells, small seashells from the Indian Ocean that served as money in much of West Africa. A captain might wait for weeks on the coast while he gathered a full cargo, and the longer he waited, the more of his crew fell sick. As the demand for captives grew, so did the prices. What rulers wanted most were guns and the power over their neighbors that guns could give.

    The captives themselves had often been marched for weeks from the interior. Most had been taken prisoner in war or raids, and some had been seized for debt or as punishment for a crime. At the coast they were held in forts and in pens built for the purpose, often in cells with little light or air, until a ship arrived to take them.

    Not every ruler agreed. Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo, wrote to the king of Portugal in 1526. He complained that Portuguese merchants were kidnapping his people, even members of noble families, and emptying his kingdom. The king of Portugal never stopped the trade. Afonso's letter shows that the trade was criticized from the beginning, including by African rulers.

    Afonso was no enemy of Portugal. He had become a Christian and taken a Christian name, he had learned Portuguese, and he sent his son Henrique to be educated in Portugal, where Henrique became a bishop. He wanted Portuguese teachers, priests, and craftsmen. What he discovered was that the same merchants who brought him help also bought his people, and that his own nobles were tempted to sell captives for foreign goods. In his letter he asked the king to send only teachers and priests and to take the traders away. The request went nowhere.

    Part 3

    The Triangle and Its Numbers

    Chapter 3The Triangle and Its Numbers
    Chapter 3

    The Triangle and Its Numbers

    Historians often picture the trade as a triangle. Ships left European ports such as Bristol, Liverpool, Nantes, and Lisbon loaded with trade goods. They sailed to Africa and exchanged those goods for captives. They then crossed the Atlantic to sell the captives in the Americas, and loaded sugar, tobacco, and other crops for the voyage home. In practice, many voyages did not follow that shape. Ships sailed directly between Brazil and Angola, for example.

    The winds shaped the triangle, because a sailing ship could not go where it liked. Sailing south from Europe, ships caught the trade winds and currents that bore them down the African coast, and from there the same winds drove them westward to the Caribbean. The voyage home followed a different route, north along the American coast with the Gulf Stream and then eastward on the prevailing westerlies. A map of the trade routes is mostly a map of the winds.

    A voyage began with money borrowed and invested. Merchants in Bristol or Liverpool paid for the ship, the crew, and the trade goods, often with funds from many investors who shared the risk. Each leg of the triangle was meant to pay for the next. The goods bought captives, the captives bought sugar and tobacco, and the cargo sold at home for more than the whole voyage had cost. Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried nearly half of all the Africans who crossed the Atlantic, and British ships carried about a quarter.

    The numbers are hard to take in. Between the 1500s and the 1860s, about twelve and a half million Africans were loaded onto ships. More than ten million survived the voyage. Most went to Brazil and the Caribbean, where sugar was king. A much smaller share, roughly four hundred thousand, went to the lands that became the United States. The sugar islands were so deadly that planters bought new workers rather than expect the old ones to live long enough to raise families.

    Part 4

    The Middle Passage

    Chapter 4The Middle Passage
    Chapter 4

    The Middle Passage

    The crossing from Africa to the Americas was the middle leg of the triangle, and the name Middle Passage has stuck. It took from five to ten weeks. Captives were chained in the hold, packed so closely that they could hardly turn over. The air was foul and the heat was terrible. Dysentery and smallpox spread quickly. On average about one person in eight died on the way, and sailors died at similar rates. Captains had a financial reason to keep captives alive, but they also packed their ships tightly in order to carry more.

    Food and air were a constant worry. Ships' surgeons recorded meals of boiled rice, beans, and yams, served from tubs, with a little water twice a day. In good weather captives were brought on deck in daylight, and some captains had them made to move about, which they called dancing, to keep their limbs from stiffening. Those who refused were whipped. When sickness struck, the dead were thrown overboard, and the living stayed chained beside the dying.

    One survivor wrote down what he saw. Olaudah Equiano described the voyage in his book of 1789: "The closeness of the place, and the heat of the climate, added to the number in the ship, which was so crowded that each had scarcely room to turn himself, almost suffocated us." (Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, 1789, Chapter 2.) He went on to describe air so bad that it was hard to breathe, a sickness in which many died, and the groans of the dying. Equiano was a boy, and the crew kept him on deck and did not put him in chains, and that is partly why he could see so much of what happened to the others.

    Enslaved people fought back. There were revolts on perhaps one voyage in ten, and some captives refused to eat. Others jumped overboard. In 1781 the captain of a ship called the Zong had about 130 sick captives thrown into the sea so that his owners could claim the loss from their insurers. A court heard the case as a dispute about money. When the story came out in England, many people were horrified. At the end of the voyage, captives were sold at auction in the port, and families were broken up. Unlike an indentured servant, whose time would end, an enslaved person was bound for life, and so were the children.

    Part 5

    Life on the Plantation

    Chapter 5Life on the Plantation
    Chapter 5

    Life on the Plantation

    On a sugar plantation, work began at dawn and ended long after dark. During harvest, workers cut cane and tended the mill for sixteen or eighteen hours a day, since the juice would spoil if it sat. Overseers, called drivers, enforced the pace with whips. Some enslaved people were also skilled craftsmen, cooks, or household servants, but nearly all lived under constant threat of punishment. On the sugar islands deaths outnumbered births, so planters kept buying new workers.

    Planters divided the work by strength. The first gang, made up of the strongest adults, did the hardest labor, cutting cane and digging the holes for new plants. A second gang followed with lighter tasks. A third gang of children and older people weeded and gathered grass for the animals. On many islands the owners also gave the enslaved small plots of ground, which they worked on their one free day. What they grew fed their families, and some of it went to Sunday markets. The plots saved the planter the cost of feeding his workers. They also left the enslaved a little ground and a little trade of their own, and a few saved enough to buy their freedom.

    Governments wrote laws to control the system. Barbados passed a slave code in 1661 that later served as a model for other English colonies. In 1685 the king of France issued the Code Noir for his Caribbean colonies. It ordered that enslaved people be baptized and limited some punishments, but it also treated them as property that could be bought, sold, and inherited. Still, the enslaved held on to their languages, music, and religious practices. Some escaped to the mountains and formed communities of their own. In Jamaica these free communities, known as Maroons, fought the British to a standstill and forced them to sign a treaty in 1739.

    Part 6

    The Long Fight to End It

    Chapter 6The Long Fight to End It
    Chapter 6

    The Long Fight to End It

    Opposition came slowly. The Quakers, a Christian group, began condemning slavery in the 1600s. In the 1700s a growing number of Britons joined them. These abolitionists included Thomas Clarkson, who gathered evidence, William Wilberforce, who fought for a ban in Parliament, and Olaudah Equiano, a formerly enslaved African who wrote about his experience. They printed pamphlets, organized boycotts of sugar, and petitioned Parliament by the thousands. In 1789 Equiano published his life story, and it sold widely and persuaded many readers that the people in the holds of the ships were human beings with families, memories, and hopes like their own. Planters and shipowners fought back, claiming that abolition would ruin Britain's economy. Their persistence was an example of courage that went against the interests of powerful men.

    Law and evidence both moved the case. In 1772 Lord Mansfield heard the case of James Somerset, an enslaved man whom his owner had brought to England and meant to send to Jamaica. Mansfield ruled that Somerset could not be forced out of the country, and many people read the decision as saying that slavery had no basis in English law, though it went on in the colonies. In 1787 the abolitionists formed a committee in London. Clarkson traveled from port to port, questioning sailors and collecting chains and handcuffs to show Parliament what the trade used. A printed plan of a slave ship called the Brookes, which showed the hold packed with hundreds of tiny figures, was pinned to walls across Britain. By one estimate, as many as three hundred thousand people gave up sugar for a time.

    Wilberforce took the cause into Parliament and brought bills against the trade year after year. They failed. The war with France that began in 1793 made many members wary of any reform, and the trade had powerful friends among the merchants of Liverpool and Bristol. Josiah Wedgwood, the potter, made a medallion for the cause that showed a kneeling African in chains beneath the words "Am I not a man and a brother?" People wore it as a pin and had it set into snuffboxes.

    Saint-Domingue was the greatest test of the system. By 1789 the French colony was the richest in the Caribbean, with about half a million enslaved people working its sugar and coffee estates, and the enslaved far outnumbered the free colonists. A planter class so outnumbered could keep control only by terror. When news of the French Revolution reached the island, the colonists quarreled among themselves over who would hold power, and the enslaved saw an opening.

    Enslaved people also freed themselves. In 1791 the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue rose against their masters. After years of war, they won, and in 1804 they declared the independent nation of Haiti. Their greatest general, Toussaint Louverture, had been born into slavery. When Napoleon sent a large army to retake the colony in 1802, yellow fever killed most of its soldiers. In 1807 Britain banned its slave trade, and the United States did the same in 1808. Britain abolished slavery itself in its empire in 1833. Parliament paid twenty million pounds to the slave owners for their loss. The formerly enslaved received nothing, and many were first required to work for their old masters for several more years as apprentices. Brazil was the last to act, in 1888. Remember what you saw in this module. Sugar made fortunes, and the demand for labor drew millions of Africans across the Atlantic into bondage. Ending the trade took the work of many people over many decades.
